pages.subtitle: Mary appeared to a humble Native man in Mexico and left her image on his cloak.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: Tepeyac Hill, in what is now Mexico City

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Honored by the Church for centuries, with her own feast day on December 12

pages.intro: In December 1531, a Native man named Juan Diego was walking to Mass near Mexico City. On a hill called Tepeyac, Mary appeared to him and asked for a church to be built there. The bishop asked for a sign. Juan Diego brought him roses in his cloak, and an image of Mary appeared on the cloth. People still honor that image today.
story_paragraphs: Almost 500 years ago, a Native man named Juan Diego lived near the place we now call Mexico City. He and his wife had been baptized a few years earlier.

According to tradition, Juan Diego was walking to Mass on December 9, 1531. As he crossed a hill called Tepeyac, Mary appeared to him. She asked him to go to the bishop and ask for a church to be built on that hill.

Juan Diego went to the bishop, Juan de Zumárraga. The bishop was not sure what to think. Mary told Juan Diego to go back and try again. The next day, the bishop asked for a sign to show that the message was true.

Then Juan Diego's uncle, Juan Bernardino, became very sick. On December 12, Juan Diego went to find a priest for him. Mary appeared again. She told Juan Diego that his uncle would get well. Then she told him to gather roses from the hill and carry them to the bishop.
It was winter, yet roses were blooming there. They were a kind that grew in Castile, the part of Spain the bishop came from. Juan Diego gathered them in his cloak, which was called a tilma.

When Juan Diego opened his tilma in front of the bishop, the roses fell out. On the inside of the cloak was an image of Mary. The bishop ordered a church to be built on Tepeyac Hill. The story also says that Mary appeared to Juan Bernardino, and he became well again.
Juan Diego spent the rest of his life in a small home beside the church. The image on his tilma is still kept in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

Over the centuries, love for Our Lady of Guadalupe spread across Mexico and far beyond. In 1754, Pope Benedict XIV gave her a feast day, December 12. Later popes named her the patroness of Latin America and of all the Americas.

pages.subtitle: Mary appeared to three shepherd children in Portugal and asked the world to pray for peace.

quick_facts.label: Who saw her
quick_facts.value: Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins, Saints Francisco and Jacinta Marto

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Declared worthy of belief by the local bishop in 1930

pages.intro: In 1917, three children were watching their families' sheep near the village of Fatima, in Portugal. A lady brighter than the sun appeared to them. She came six times and asked them to pray the Rosary every day for peace. On her last visit, she said, "I am the Lady of the Rosary." Two of the children, Francisco and Jacinta, are now saints.
story_paragraphs: In 1917, a terrible war was being fought across Europe. In the little village of Aljustrel, near Fatima in Portugal, three children took care of their families' sheep. Lúcia was 10 years old. Her cousins, Francisco and Jacinta Marto, were 8 and 7.

On May 13, 1917, the children were with their sheep at a place called the Cova da Iria. Suddenly they saw a lady dressed in white, standing above a small oak tree. Lúcia later said she was "brighter than the sun." When Lúcia asked where she was from, the lady answered, "I am from Heaven."
The lady asked the children to come back on the 13th day of each month for six months. She told them, "Pray the Rosary every day, in order to obtain peace for the world, and the end of the war."

The children kept coming, and more and more people came with them. Not everyone believed them. On August 13, a local official took the three children away and kept them for two days, so they missed the meeting. The lady appeared to them a few days later, on August 19, at a place called Valinhos.

On October 13, a huge crowd gathered at the Cova da Iria, at least 50,000 people. The lady told the children, "I am the Lady of the Rosary." She asked people to stop offending God. A newspaper reported that the sun seemed to "dance" in the sky that day.

Soon after, a sickness called influenza spread through the country. Francisco died on April 4, 1919. Jacinta died on February 20, 1920. Lúcia became a religious sister. She lived a long life of prayer and died in 2005.

The bishop studied what had happened. On October 13, 1930, he declared the children's visions worthy of belief. On May 13, 2017, one hundred years after the first apparition, Pope Francis declared Francisco and Jacinta saints at Fatima.

pages.student_title: Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal
pages.subtitle: In a chapel in Paris, Mary showed a young sister a medal to share with the world.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: A convent chapel on the Rue du Bac in Paris, France

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: The medal was made with the Church's approval in 1832

pages.intro: In 1830, a young sister named Catherine Labouré was living in a convent in Paris, France. One night, Mary appeared to her in the chapel. A few months later, Mary appeared again and showed her a medal to be made and shared. Catherine kept her part in the story secret for 46 years. Today, people all over the world wear the Miraculous Medal.
story_paragraphs: Catherine Labouré was born on May 2, 1806, in a village in France. Her mother died when Catherine was nine years old. When she grew up, Catherine chose to become a religious sister. On April 21, 1830, she joined the Daughters of Charity at their house on a street in Paris called the Rue du Bac.

On the night of July 18, 1830, a child's voice woke Catherine and led her to the chapel. There she saw Mary, seated in a chair. Mary told her, "My child, the good God wishes to charge you with a mission."
On November 27, 1830, during evening prayer in the chapel, Catherine saw Mary again. This time, Mary was standing on a globe, and rays of light streamed from rings on her fingers.

Around Mary, Catherine saw words in the shape of an oval: "O Mary conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee." Then Catherine was shown the back of the medal. She saw the letter M with a cross above it, two hearts, and twelve stars. She heard the words, "Have a medal struck after this model." To strike a medal means to make it out of metal.

Catherine told only one person, her priest, Father Aladel. With the Church's approval, the first medals were made in 1832 and given out in Paris. So many people said they received help from God while wearing it that they began calling it the "Miraculous Medal."

Catherine never told the other sisters that she was the one who had seen Mary. For 46 years, she quietly cared for elderly and poor people. Only in 1876, shortly before she died, did she tell her superior. Catherine died on December 31, 1876.
Pope Pius XII declared Catherine a saint on July 27, 1947.

pages.subtitle: On a rainy evening in Ireland, fifteen people saw Mary, Saint Joseph, and Saint John beside their village church.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: Knock, in the west of Ireland

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Church inquiries found the witnesses trustworthy

pages.intro: On a rainy evening in 1879, people in the Irish village of Knock saw something wonderful at the end wall of their church. Mary was there, with Saint Joseph and Saint John. Beside them was an altar with a lamb and a cross. Fifteen people watched for about two hours. No one in the vision spoke a single word.
story_paragraphs: Knock is a small village in the west of Ireland. In 1879, the people there were poor, and life was hard. On the evening of August 21, 1879, rain was pouring down. Some villagers noticed figures standing at the gable of the parish church. A gable is the end wall of a building, the part that comes to a point under the roof.

The people came closer. They saw Mary, wearing a white cloak and a crown. Saint Joseph stood on her right, dressed in white. On her other side was Saint John the Evangelist, one of the twelve apostles and the writer of a Gospel.
Beside the three figures was an altar. On the altar stood a lamb, with a cross behind it, and angels were around it. In the Bible, Jesus is called the Lamb of God.

More neighbors came, until fifteen people were watching. They stayed for about two hours in the rain. No one in the vision spoke. One of the witnesses was an 11-year-old boy named Patrick Hill. He said, "They said nothing, but as we approached, they seemed to go back a little towards the gable." He also said the figures looked "full and round as if they had a body and were alive."
A few weeks later, in October 1879, the archbishop sent three priests to question the witnesses. They reported that the testimony of all, taken as a whole, was "trustworthy and satisfactory."
In 1936, the Church asked again. One of the last witnesses, Mary Byrne O'Connell, was old and sick in bed. She swore that what she had told as a young woman was true. She died six weeks later.
Pope John Paul II came to pray at Knock in 1979, one hundred years after the apparition. In 2021, Pope Francis gave Knock a special title: an International Eucharistic and Marian Shrine.

pages.subtitle: High in the mountains of France, two children met a beautiful lady who was crying.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: A mountain near the village of La Salette, France

quick_facts.label: Who saw her
quick_facts.value: Maximin Giraud, age 11, and Mélanie Calvat, age 14

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Approved by the local bishop in 1851

pages.intro: On September 19, 1846, two children were watching cows on a mountain in France. They saw a bright light, and inside it a beautiful lady, sitting with her face in her hands. She was crying. She told the children that people had forgotten God, and she asked everyone to pray and to come back to him. Then she rose into the air and was gone.
story_paragraphs: Maximin Giraud was 11 years old, and Mélanie Calvat was 14. They lived in the mountains of France, near a village called La Salette. Their job was to watch over cows as they grazed.
On Saturday, September 19, 1846, the two children were high on the mountain with their herds. Suddenly they saw a ball of light, as bright as if the sun had fallen to the ground.

Inside the light sat a lady. Her elbows rested on her knees, and her face was in her hands. She was crying. Then she stood up and said, "Come closer, my children; don't be afraid. I am here to tell you great news."

The lady was tall and shining. She wore a long dress, an apron, and a shawl. Roses were around her head, her shawl, and her feet. On a chain around her neck hung a crucifix. Next to the figure of Jesus were a hammer and a pair of pincers, the tool used to pull out nails.

The lady cried the whole time she spoke. She was sad because people were working on Sundays instead of going to Mass, and because they used her Son's name in angry words. She asked the children if they said their prayers. "Hardly ever," they answered. She told them to pray every morning and every night.

She warned that hard times and hunger were coming. But she also gave hope. If people turned back to God, she said, there would be plenty of food again. The lady began speaking in French. When she saw that the children did not understand, she spoke in the local language they used at home.

Her last words were, "Well, my children, you will make this known to all my people." Then she walked up the path, rose into the air, and disappeared into the light. The children told what they had seen. The bishop studied it carefully for five years. In 1851, he declared that the apparition "bears within itself all the characteristics of truth."

pages.subtitle: In the woods of Wisconsin, Mary asked a young woman to teach children about God.

quick_facts.label: Where
quick_facts.value: Champion, Wisconsin, in the United States

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Approved by the local bishop in 2010

pages.intro: In 1859, a young woman named Adele Brise was walking through the woods in Wisconsin. A lady dressed in shining white appeared between two trees. She said she was the Queen of Heaven. She asked Adele to pray for sinners and to teach the children about God. Adele spent the rest of her life doing just that. This is the first approved apparition of Mary in the United States.
story_paragraphs: Adele Brise was born on January 30, 1831, in the country of Belgium. When she was a young child, she lost the sight of one eye. In 1855, her family crossed the ocean to start a new life in Wisconsin, in the United States. Their new home was in the woods, and the nearest church was 11 miles away.
One day in early October 1859, Adele was walking through the woods. She saw a lady in white standing between two trees. Then the lady was gone. Adele did not know what to think.
On Sunday, October 9, Adele was on her way to Mass. She saw the lady again, between the same two trees. After Mass, Adele walked home with two companions, and the lady appeared a third time.
The lady was dressed in dazzling white, with a yellow sash around her waist and a crown of stars around her head. This time Adele asked, "In God's name, who are you, and what do you want of me?"

The lady answered, "I am the Queen of Heaven who prays for the conversion of sinners, and I wish you to do the same." Then she gave Adele a job: "Gather the children in this wild country and teach them what they should know for salvation." She added, "Go and fear nothing, I will help you."

Adele obeyed. She went from house to house, walking as far as 50 miles, to teach children how to pray and to know and love God. Later, other women joined her. With help from her Belgian neighbors, a school, a chapel, and a convent were built near the place where Mary had appeared.

In October 1871, a terrible fire swept through the forests of Wisconsin. Adele and many neighbors gathered at the chapel grounds and walked around them, praying through the night. Rain came early in the morning, and the chapel grounds were not burned.
Adele died on July 5, 1896. On December 8, 2010, Bishop David Ricken declared the apparitions worthy of belief.

pages.subtitle: On winter nights in Belgium, Mary came to a poor family's garden and called herself the Virgin of the Poor.

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Approved by the local bishop in 1949

pages.intro: In the winter of 1933, an 11-year-old girl named Mariette Beco lived with her family in a small house near Banneux, Belgium. One evening, she saw a lady standing in the garden. The lady came eight times. She led Mariette to a spring of water and said, "I am the Virgin of the Poor." She asked for a little chapel and for much prayer.
story_paragraphs: Mariette Beco was born on March 25, 1921. She was the oldest of seven children. Her family lived in a small house near the village of Banneux, in Belgium, and they did not have much.
On Sunday evening, January 15, 1933, Mariette saw a lady standing in the garden. The lady waved for her to come. But Mariette's mother would not let her go outside.
Three days later, the lady came again. This time Mariette went out. The lady led her along the road to a small spring of water and said that the spring was set apart for her.
The next evening, Mariette asked, "Who are you, beautiful lady?" The lady answered, "I am the Virgin of the Poor." Then she said the spring was "for all Nations… to relieve the sick."

On January 20, Mariette asked what the lady wanted. She said, "I would like a little chapel." For three weeks, the lady did not come. Mariette kept going out to the garden to pray in the cold. On February 11, the lady came back. She said, "I come to relieve suffering."
A priest had told Mariette to ask for a sign. When she did, the lady answered, "Believe in me, I will believe in you." Again and again, she asked Mariette to pray a lot.

On March 2, the lady came for the last time. She said, "I am the Mother of the Saviour, Mother of God. Pray a lot." She laid her hands on Mariette and said goodbye. That summer, the little chapel the lady had asked for was built. The bishop studied what had happened for many years. On August 22, 1949, Bishop Kerkhofs of Liège declared that Mary had truly appeared at Banneux.

pages.subtitle: Five children in Belgium saw Mary 33 times, and she showed them her heart of gold.

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Approved by the local bishop in 1949

pages.intro: In the winter of 1932, five children in the town of Beauraing, Belgium, saw a lady in white near their school. She came back 33 times. She asked them to be good and to pray. Near the end, the children saw her heart shining like gold. On her last visit, she said, "I am the Mother of God, the Queen of heaven."
story_paragraphs: Beauraing is a town in Belgium. In 1932, five children from two families lived there. In the Voisin family were Fernande, who was 15, Gilberte, who was 13, and Albert, who was 11. In the Degeimbre family were Andrée, who was 14, and her little sister Gilberte, who was 9.

On the evening of November 29, 1932, four of the children walked to a school run by religious sisters to meet Gilberte Voisin. As they waited, Albert pointed toward a railroad bridge near the school. A lady in white was there, and she seemed to be walking in the air. The children ran home, amazed.

They came back the next evenings, and the lady came too. Most of the time, she appeared in the school garden, near a hawthorn tree. She wore a long white dress, and rays of light shone like a crown around her head. When she came, the children dropped to their knees.
Albert asked her, "Are you the Immaculate Virgin?" The lady smiled and nodded. Then he asked, "What do you want?" She answered, "Always be good."
At first, the head sister of the school did not believe the children, and she locked the garden gate. Doctors came to watch and test the children. More and more people came, too.
On December 17, the lady asked for a chapel to be built. From December 29 on, the children saw her heart shining as if it were made of gold. That is why she is called the Virgin of the Golden Heart.

The last apparition was on January 3, 1933. About 20,000 people were there. The lady said, "I will convert sinners. I am the Mother of God, the Queen of heaven." To Fernande she said, "Do you love my Son? Do you love me? Then sacrifice yourself for me."
The bishop studied everything for years. On July 2, 1949, the Bishop of Namur approved the apparitions.

pages.subtitle: Mary appeared to three students in Rwanda and called her children to pray, to love, and to forgive.

quick_facts.label: Who saw her
quick_facts.value: Three students: Alphonsine, Nathalie, and Marie Claire

quick_facts.label: Church says
quick_facts.value: Approved by the local bishop in 2001

pages.intro: Kibeho is a village in Rwanda, a country in Africa. On November 28, 1981, a 16-year-old student named Alphonsine saw a beautiful lady at her school. The lady called herself the Mother of the Word. Soon two more students saw her too. Mary asked everyone to turn back to God, to pray, and to love one another. In 2001, the bishop said that Mary truly appeared there.
story_paragraphs: Kibeho is a small village in the hills of Rwanda, a country in Africa. In 1981, there was a school for girls there.

On November 28, 1981, a 16-year-old student named Alphonsine Mumureke was at the school when she saw a lady. The lady told her, in Alphonsine's own language, "Ndi Nyina wa Jambo." That means, "I am the Mother of the Word." The Word is a name for Jesus, so this is another way of saying "Mother of God."

At first, many of the other students and teachers did not believe Alphonsine. Then, on January 12, 1982, a 17-year-old student named Nathalie Mukamazimpaka saw the lady too. On March 2, a third student, Marie Claire Mukangango, who was 21, also saw her.

Mary told the girls they did not need to be afraid of their mother. She asked people to change their hearts and turn back to God. She asked them to pray, especially the Rosary, to be humble, to love their neighbors, and to forgive. She also asked for a chapel to be built.
Mary taught Marie Claire a special prayer called the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows. It remembers seven sad times in Mary's life.
On August 15, 1982, something different happened. The girls saw Mary crying, and they saw frightening things. They cried too.

Twelve years later, in 1994, a terrible time came to Rwanda. In just a few months, a great many people were killed. It is called a genocide. Many people died at Kibeho, too. The bishop later wrote that what the girls saw in 1982 seemed to have been a warning.

The Church studied the apparitions for twenty years. Doctors and experts in the faith questioned the three young women. On June 29, 2001, Bishop Augustin Misago declared, "Yes, the Virgin Mary appeared at Kibeho on November 28th, 1981 and in the months that followed."
